title: Causal confusion in quantum systems: distinguishing direct cause and common cause
authors: Krisztina Tolotti, Riley Blank-Matthews, Arthur J. Parzygnat
abstract: The joint expectation values of quantum observables measured by two parties typically depend on the causal structure of the measurement protocol. The two causal structures we investigate here are the direct-cause scenario, in which a single quantum state is measured twice in series with a general quantum channel between measurements, and the common-cause scenario, in which a shared bipartite quantum state is measured in parallel. Through a variety of examples of qubit channels with tunable parameters, we identify the full set of input states where the direct-cause joint expectation values of Pauli observables coincide with those obtained from a common cause, a situation that we call causal confusion. More generally, for arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum systems and light-touch observables, we prove that a channel exhibits causal confusion for some input state if and only if it is a positive-partial-transpose (PPT) channel, thereby endowing PPT channels with a new operational meaning in terms of causal confusion. Using this result, we characterize the set of qubit channels for which there exists an input state leading to causal confusion as the set of entanglement-breaking channels.
summary: This paper tackles the problem of quantum causality by defining 'causal confusion'—when measurement data cannot distinguish between a shared common cause and a sequential direct cause. The authors prove that this confusion occurs if and only if the underlying quantum channel possesses the PPT property, providing a new operational meaning for PPT channels.
main_problem: The paper investigates 'causal confusion,' which is the situation where joint expectation values measured in a spatial (common-cause) quantum scenario coincide with those from a temporal (direct-cause) quantum scenario.
main_result: It establishes that for general systems, a quantum channel exhibits causal confusion for some input state if and only if it is a Positive-Partial-Transpose (PPT) channel, and for qubits, this condition is equivalent to the channel being entanglement-breaking.
method: The authors compare joint expectation values calculated under two distinct causal models—a shared bipartite state (spatial) versus sequential measurement through a quantum channel (temporal)—using Pauli observables.
model_or_system: The study uses general finite-dimensional quantum systems and focuses on local measurements performed by two parties (Alice and Bob) on quantum states, analyzing the structure of quantum channels connecting these measurements.
key_observables: Joint expectation values of Pauli observables ($\sigma_j \otimes \sigma_k$), which are used to distinguish between the spatial and temporal correlation structures.
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the properties of the quantum channel $E$ (e.g., PPT, entanglement-breaking) and the choice of input state $ho$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to 'light-touch observables' and uses the Lüders' update rule for the temporal scenario in qubit examples.

paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the spatial and temporal measurement scenarios, demonstrating the conditions for causal confusion using qubit examples, and culminating in general structural theorems linking confusion to PPT and entanglement-breaking properties.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous operational definition for PPT channels by linking them to a fundamental concept in quantum causality, which is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum information processing and measurement theory.
